'''Kim E. Jelfs''' is a [[computational chemistry | computational chemist]] based at [[Imperial College London]] who was one of the recipients of the [[Harrison-Meldola Memorial Prizes]] in 2018. She develops software to predict the structures and properties of molecular systems for renewable energy.

==Early life and education==
Jelfs studied chemistry at [[University College London]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/171915/imperial-strengthens-expertise-computational-chemistry-drug/|title=Imperial strengthens expertise in computational chemistry and drug discovery {{!}} Imperial News {{!}} Imperial College London|work=Imperial News|access-date=2018-06-01|language=en-GB}}</ref> For her final year project, Jelfs worked at the [[Royal Institution]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/HarrisonMeldolaMemorialPrizes/Index.asp|title=RSC Harrison-Meldola Memorial Prizes|website=www.rsc.org|language=en|access-date=2018-06-01}}</ref> She earned her PhD in 2010, working with Ben Slater on modelling the growth of [[Zeolite|zeolitic]] materials.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite thesis|url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/19480/|title=Modelling the growth of zeolitic materials|last=K.E.|first=Jelfs|date=2010-03-28|website=discovery.ucl.ac.uk|access-date=2018-06-01|type=Doctoral}}</ref>

==Research and career==
After completing her PhD Jelfs joined the [[University of Barcelona]], working with Stefan Bromley. She moved to the [[University of Liverpool]], working as a postdoctoral researcher with [[Matthew Rosseinsky]] and [[Andrew Ian Cooper]].<ref name=":1" /> At the [[University of Liverpool]] Jelfs characterised the structure of porous materials.<ref name=":1" /> She was funded by an [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] Programme Grant.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/cooper-group/people/kim-jelfs/|title=Kim Jelfs - Cooper Group - University of Liverpool|website=www.liverpool.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=2018-06-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.directedassembly.co.uk/phases.html|title=Phases 1, 2, 3 +|website=www.directedassembly.co.uk|language=en-gb|access-date=2018-06-01}}</ref>

In 2013 she joined [[Imperial College London]] as a [[Royal Society University Research Fellowship|Royal Society University Research Fellow]].<ref name=":0" /> In 2015 she was awarded a [[European Research Council]] Starting Grant, which provides €1.5 million funding for five years of materials discovery.<ref>{{Cite Her research will consider porous molecules, organic small molecules and polymers.<ref name=":2" /> She uses computational models to predict the relationships between structure and properties.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www.jelfs-group.org/research-1/|title=Research|website=Jelfs Computational Materials Group|language=en-US|access-date=2018-06-01|archive-date=2018-05-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180519074210/http://www.jelfs-group.org/research-1|url-status=dead}}</ref> The models can also be used to predict the properties of amorphous frameworks and porous molecules.<ref name=":3" /> Her group identified the 20 most probable topologies for porous cage molecules, which can be In 2018 Jelfs was awarded the [[Harrison-Meldola Memorial Prizes|Harrison-Meldola Memorial Prize]] from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name=":1" /> She was also awarded an [[Imperial College London]] President's Award for Outstanding Early Career Research.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/186453/outstanding-research-projects-people-recognised-2018|title=Outstanding research projects and people recognised in 2018 President's Awards {{!}} Imperial News {{!}} Imperial College London|work=Imperial News|access-date=2018-06-01|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/186055/top-honours-three-imperial-chemists/|title=Top honours for three Imperial chemists {{!}} Imperial News {{!}} Imperial College London|work=Imperial News|access-date=2018-06-01|language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2019, she was awarded a Philip Leverhulme Prize in Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Philip Leverhulme Prizes 2019 {{!}} The Leverhulme Trust|url=https://www.leverhulme.ac.uk/philip-leverhulme-prizes-2019|access-date=2020-12-15|website=www.leverhulme.ac.uk}}</ref> In 2025, Jelfs was awarded the Royal Society of Chemistry's [[Corday–Morgan Prize|Corday-Morgan Prize]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Corday-Morgan Mid-Career Prizes for Chemistry |url=https://www.rsc.org/standards-and-recognition/prizes/research-and-innovation-prizes/corday-morgan-mid-career-prizes-for-chemistry |access-date=2026-02-25 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |language=en}}</ref>.
